newsitem.title: UK: Direct Line blames tough market conditions.
newsitem.headline: Direct Line blames tough market conditions.

text.p: Britain's low cost telephone-based insurer Direct Line on Thursday blamed a sharp decline in profits on intense competition in motor insurance where prices have fallen, but argued rivals were suffering more than it was.

The Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) subsidiary, which since its launch just over ten years ago has grown rapidly to become one of the country's biggest motor insurers, reported an 86 million pounds slide in full year pre-tax profits to 26.5 million.
"This has been an extremely competitive year for motor and home insurance," said RBS chairman Lord Younger. But he added that Direct Line would benefit once premium rates recovered.
Severe winter weather and a 16.7 percent rise in the average cost of personal injury claims contributed to a 25 percent increase in general insurance claims to 562 million pounds.

"The deterioration had been well flagged and the company had given the causes of that deterioration," said Merrill Lynch insurance analyst Steven Bird, who left his forecast for 1997 pre-tax profits unchanged at 28 million to 30 million pounds.

Direct Line has like many of its competitors in the British insurance market suffered from a 25 percent decline in rates over the last three years, with competition intensfied by the telephone sales techniques first employed by Direct Line itself.

Motor insurance premiums fell five percent during 1995-96 and the total number of motor policies in force fell by 30,000 from 2.2 million, a small but significant first time drop for Direct Line, which had based its strategy on grabbing as much market share as possible by undercutting competitors on price.

While Direct Line's founder and chairman Peter Wood noted motor insurance rates were beginning to recover, he said it could be two years before many of those insurers underwriting motor at a loss began to write business profitably again.

"We'll put our foot back on the accelerator when the market sees sense," he told reporters. Wood now spends one week in four in the U.S., where he is launching a new insurer called Direct Response, expected to sell its first policy by June next year.
Ian Chippendale, chief executive of Direct Line Insurance, which handles motor and home insurance but not life, said relatively low expenses gave the firm an "enormous advantage".
"Our competitors will be suffering," he told Reuters in an interview. "We've got forty percent of the market's operating costs, so we're in a much stronger competitive position."
Operating cost per policy has fallen from 48 to 45 pounds and staff numbers at Direct Line Insurance, which handles motor and home insurance sales, shrank by 160 to 2,690 over the year.

In addition, Direct Line is poised to complete a project linking all its call centres to a common telephone response network. The insurer will within days be able to direct all claims to whichever regional centre can take the call first.

Direct Line's financial services operation made solid progress. The value of its mortgage book rose from 140 million pounds to 550 million and newly launched instant access savings netted 250 million. Personal loans were over 100 million pounds.
The group is expected to begin working soon with mutual life assurer Scottish Widows, which is in co-operation talks with RBS. The venture may involve the marketing of personal pensions.
